subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage: I'm Pradeep, and I sit opposite Siddharth in the Leeds office. At the team lunch on Wednesday, two colleagues took turns imitating how he says "schedule," and laughed. He smiled thinly and ate faster. Afterwards nobody invited him to the pub, as usual. I couldn't tell how much it hurt; he only said, "It's a bit tiring." On Friday he asked one of them, calmly, in the corridor, to stop the impressions. The colleague shrugged it off, and it happened again. Siddharth wrote it down with dates and sent it to HR. Then he joined the Saturday five-a-side that some of us play. "Their bias isn't my flaw," he told me, almost to himself, "but I still have to make it stop."

qa.q: What did the two colleagues imitate at the team lunch?
qa.a: They imitated how Siddharth says "schedule."

qa.q: What might Siddharth have felt during the lunch, given his thin smile and how fast he ate?
qa.a: He may have been hurt and tried to hide it, but Pradeep couldn't tell how much it hurt. A smile is a cue, not proof.

qa.q: What did Siddharth do after the impressions happened again, and why does it help?
qa.a: He wrote it down with dates and sent it to HR, so there is a record for a proper report. He also found friendlier company at the five-a-side.

qa.q: How might the colleague who shrugged it off have seen the impressions?
qa.a: Possibly as a harmless joke, although Siddharth clearly experienced it as mockery. The repeat suggests the request wasn't taken seriously.

grounding: Stereotypes and accent mockery in a new country; naming it, calmly asking for it to stop, finding supportive people and reporting discrimination.

subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage: On his third Saturday in Kolkata, Tanvir let the tram carry him past his stop just to see where it ended. He had already learned to say "khub bhalo" to the paan-shop owner and tried mishti doi from a clay pot, wincing at the sweetness and then asking for another. His colleague Damini took him to see the festival lights and explained why everyone dressed the way they did, and he asked so many questions that she laughed. He started leaving work later, like his team. But every Sunday he still called his mother in Hyderabad, and he cooked his own biryani for the flatmates, who lined up for seconds. "I'm collecting, not swapping," he told Damini.

qa.q: What did Tanvir cook for his flatmates?
qa.a: He cooked his own biryani for the flatmates.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir tell Damini "I'm collecting, not swapping"?
qa.a: Tanvir wants to add new customs and tastes without giving up his own. He is curious but feels no need to drop where he comes from.

qa.q: How can Tanvir decide what to adopt and what to keep?
qa.a: Adopt what helps, like the local greeting and the team's working hours, and stay rooted in what matters to him, like the Sunday calls and his own cooking.

qa.q: How does Damini seem to see Tanvir's many questions?
qa.a: She laughed, so she seems amused and welcoming, and she enjoyed explaining her city.

grounding: Exploring new customs, foods and work habits with interest while staying rooted in one's own culture, without copying blindly.

subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage: I'm Saurabh. I share a flat in Toronto with Sonali, so I see her Sunday call every week. Her father's voice sounds tired down the line and her mother says "we're fine, beta," and Sonali's smile stays fixed until she hangs up. This month she stopped pretending. She told me she couldn't fly home until next spring because of a project, and she looked away as she said it. Then she got to work. She fixed calls for Wednesdays and Sundays, booked the spring visit, and asked a cousin who lives near her parents to check in. She also told her parents honestly what she could and couldn't do from here. I can't say what she felt; she still went quiet after the calls, but less.

qa.q: Which days did Sonali fix for calls with her parents?
qa.a: She fixed calls for Wednesdays and Sundays.

qa.q: What might Sonali be feeling behind her fixed smile during the calls?
qa.a: Probably worry and guilt about being far away, torn between her project and her parents. Saurabh can only guess from her looking away and going quiet.

qa.q: What else could Sonali do to help her parents from a distance?
qa.a: Keep the regular calls, stick to the spring visit, keep the cousin's local support in place and stay honest about her limits.

qa.q: How might Sonali's parents feel about the honest conversation?
qa.a: Perhaps relieved to hear the truth. Saying "we're fine, beta" hints that they may have been hiding their own worries too.

grounding: Living far from ageing parents and feeling torn: regular calls, planned visits, local support and honesty about limits instead of guilt alone.

subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage: I'm Nirmala, and I live two doors from Gurpreet's parents in Ludhiana. Every evening on the video call they sound bright: "All good here, don't worry about us." Afterwards I see Gurpreet's mother wiping the same table twice and Papa staring at the phone. Last week Gurpreet asked plainly, "Mummy, how are you really?" There was a pause, then she admitted the house felt big. Since then Gurpreet sends small things: a photo of a bad cup of tea, a voice note from the bus. Yesterday Gurpreet asked their opinion on which flat to rent, and Papa spent ten minutes giving reasons. A visit is booked for next month. I can't say what they truly feel, but the calls run longer now.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet ask the parents' opinion about?
qa.a: Gurpreet asked which flat to rent.

qa.q: Why might Gurpreet's parents say "All good here, don't worry about us"?
qa.a: They probably miss Gurpreet and hide it so as not to worry their child. The mother wiping the same table twice and Papa staring at the phone hint at this, though Nirmala can't be sure.

qa.q: What else could Gurpreet do to keep the parents close?
qa.a: Keep asking directly how they are, keep sharing small daily things, involve them in decisions and follow through on the planned visit.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when asked about the flat?
qa.a: Valued and included, since he spent ten minutes giving reasons. It gave him a real part in Gurpreet's life.

grounding: Parents miss their child and hide it behind cheerful voices; asking directly, sharing daily life, involving them in decisions and visiting.

subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage:
Charu: just landed!! my flat is empty and the SIM shop closes soon 😅
Rekha: breathe. Take the tram to the mall, there's a shop by the pharmacy. I'll send the exact stop
Rekha: also come Saturday, we're cooking for Ugadi, bring nothing
Charu: really? thank you, I was dreading the first weekend 🥺
Rekha: same when I came. Someone did this for me, so now I do it for you
Charu: what about my colleagues? they keep inviting me to trivia night
Rekha: go!! I love our group but I don't want to only ever go to the dinners from home. trivia sounds fun
Charu: ok. trivia Thursday, Ugadi Saturday
Rekha: perfect. and next year you'll help the next newcomer 🙂

qa.q: What is Rekha's group cooking for on Saturday?
qa.a: They are cooking for Ugadi.

qa.q: How does Charu feel about the first weekend, and what changes it?
qa.a: Charu was dreading the first weekend, and feels relieved and grateful when Rekha invites Charu to cook for Ugadi.

qa.q: How can Charu enjoy the group from home and still avoid living in a bubble?
qa.a: Go to the Ugadi cooking on Saturday and also say yes to the colleagues' trivia night on Thursday.

qa.q: Why might Rekha push Charu toward trivia night instead of only the group dinners?
qa.a: Rekha loves the group but does not want to only ever go to the dinners from home, and wants Charu to mix with colleagues too rather than stay in a bubble.

grounding: People from your region are a lifeline; enjoy it but mix with the wider community, and pay forward the help you got to the next newcomer.

subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage: Sit, Noor, and I'll tell you what happened when I, Hafsa, was twenty-four and working in Muscat. My employer said, "Give me your passport, I'll keep it safe." Everyone else had handed theirs over. I said no, politely, and he frowned. The overtime was never paid, and the landlord kept adding charges to the rent. So I did three things. I made copies of my passport and contract and left them with a friend. I wrote down my hours every day. And I went to the embassy, where they pointed me to legal aid. It frightened me, Noor, more than I let on. But I never gave that passport away. Whoever asks you for yours, the answer is no.

qa.q: What three things did Hafsa do?
qa.a: Hafsa left copies of the passport and contract with a friend, wrote down hours every day, and went to the embassy, which pointed to legal aid.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel while refusing to hand over the passport?
qa.a: Frightened, more than Hafsa let on, yet firm. Refusing politely while scared shows the decision was deliberate.

qa.q: What would you advise Noor if an employer asks for a passport?
qa.a: Say no, keep copies of documents with someone trusted, write down working hours and contact the embassy or legal aid.

qa.q: What would have changed for Hafsa if the passport had been handed over like everyone else's?
qa.a: Hafsa would probably have had less freedom to leave or complain, since the employer would hold the document.

grounding: Newcomers with limited rights are exploited through unpaid overtime, rent tricks and withheld passports; keep copies, contact embassy or legal aid, never surrender the passport.

subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage: Thursday evening at the community centre in Manchester, the language exchange had spilled into the kitchen. Hrithik, who grew up in Pune and now lived here, felt the old ache: back home they called him "the foreigner" these days, and here he was "the Indian guy." He stirred his tea in silence. Pankaj, who ran the sessions, sat beside him. "You look like you fit in nowhere," Pankaj said gently. "Sometimes that means you can translate for both." Nearby, a newly arrived student was struggling with a form. Hrithik walked over, explained the words in two languages, and the student's shoulders dropped. He kept eating vegetarian, by his own choice, and practised Marathi with his aunt on Sundays. "Slowly," he told himself.

qa.q: Where was the language exchange held?
qa.a: It was held at the community centre in Manchester.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel as he stirred his tea in silence?
qa.a: He felt the old ache of fitting in nowhere, called "the foreigner" back home and "the Indian guy" here.

qa.q: How can Hrithik turn his in-between place into a strength?
qa.a: Keep acting as a bridge for newcomers, keep the values he chose, keep practising Marathi and be patient with himself.

qa.q: How might the student with the form have felt when Hrithik explained it in two languages?
qa.a: Relieved, as the dropped shoulders show. Hrithik's own in-between position made him useful.

grounding: Feeling caught between two cultures and at home in neither; the in-between becomes a bridge for others, with chosen values, language practice and patience.

passage:
Tuesday night. After the doctor named the illness, Farhan lay awake with his phone, reading page after page until his heart was racing. Nothing he found told him what would happen to him.
Friday. His brother Naveen came to the hospital with him. Farhan had written eight questions on the back of an envelope, and Naveen wrote down the answers. The doctor went through the first steps one at a time and said the rest would be planned as they went. Farhan asked about a second opinion, and the doctor said that was reasonable and offered to send the records.
Two weeks later. Farhan no longer searched at night. He read the leaflet the hospital gave him and told Naveen, "One stage at a time. I can do that."

qa.q: How many questions had Farhan written on the envelope?
qa.a: Farhan had written eight questions.

qa.q: Why was Farhan's heart racing on Tuesday night?
qa.a: He was frightened about the future, and the pages he read online gave him no real answer about what would happen to him.

qa.q: What would you advise Farhan when a new worry comes up at night?
qa.a: Write it on the question list, rely on trusted sources like the hospital leaflet, and raise it at the next appointment or with Naveen.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt about being asked to come along?
qa.a: Probably trusted and useful, writing down the answers. He may have been worried himself too.

grounding: A serious diagnosis brings fear; bringing someone, writing questions, asking about a second opinion, taking it in stages and avoiding panic searching.

passage:
Dear Pradeep,
You asked how the appointment went. Dr Rao sat down, put her pen away, and explained the two options I have, including what each can and can't do and what she doesn't know yet. I admitted I'd missed some doses because the side effects scared me, and she didn't scold me; she changed how we'll manage it. When she used a word I didn't understand, I said so, and she drew a small diagram. I'll follow the plan, and I'll keep asking. I'm not handing my body over blindly; I'm part of the team. I felt steadier walking out than I have in weeks. Thank you for asking me to write it down instead of bottling it up.
Siddharth

qa.q: What did Dr Rao draw when Siddharth did not understand a word?
qa.a: Dr Rao drew a small diagram.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth admit having missed some doses?
qa.a: The side effects had scared Siddharth, and Dr Rao's honest, unhurried manner made it feel safe to share the full picture.

qa.q: What should Siddharth do if a later instruction is unclear?
qa.a: Say so and ask again, as before, keep following the plan and keep sharing full information with the doctor.

qa.q: How might Dr Rao have seen Siddharth's honesty about the doses?
qa.a: Probably as helpful, because it let the plan be adjusted to what was really happening.

grounding: A doctor who explains options honestly earns trust; sharing full information, following the plan and asking when unsure, as a partner in treatment.

passage: Six months after my diagnosis, at twenty-five, I still asked the ceiling, why me? My friends were planning trips and I was planning appointments. It felt bitter and unfair, and it was mine to feel. One evening my sister Deepika brought my tablets with a glass of water, and I snapped, "Stop hovering, I'm not a child." Her face fell. I sat with the shame for a minute, then said, "Sorry. It's not you I'm angry at." Deepika sat down and said, "I know." Afterwards I started writing furious pages in a notebook, and walking fast round the block until my legs shook instead of my voice. The anger didn't vanish, but it stopped landing on her. — Trisha

qa.q: How old was Trisha at the time of the diagnosis?
qa.a: Trisha was twenty-five.

qa.q: Why did Trisha snap at Deepika?
qa.a: The anger came from the unfairness of illness and the loss of control. Deepika was simply nearby, and Trisha said, "It's not you I'm angry at."

qa.q: What helped Trisha deal with the anger?
qa.a: Writing furious pages in a notebook and walking fast round the block gave it a safe outlet, and a quick apology repaired the moment.

qa.q: How might Deepika have felt when Trisha snapped, and afterwards?
qa.a: Hurt, since her face fell, yet understanding. Saying "I know" shows she saw the anger was not really about her. 🤍

grounding: Why me feels bitter and unfair; anger is natural, let out safely through writing and movement, and not taken out on the person caring for you.
